'''Mark Mordecai Green''' (born April 6, 1937) is an American [[chemist]], writer and professor of chemical and [[biomolecular engineering]] at the [[New York University Tandon School of Engineering]].<ref name="NYU">[http://engineering.nyu.edu/people/mark-green NYU Tandon School of Engineering], Mark Green</ref><ref>[http://catalog.poly.edu/preview_entity.php?catoid=7&ent_oid=573&returnto=618&print 2013–2014 Undergraduate and Graduate Bulletin], New York University Polytechnic School of Engineering</ref> He is best known for his extensive work on an aspect of [[stereochemistry]] involved in cooperative chirality and also for his book ''Organic Chemistry Principles in Context: A Story Telling Historical Approach'', which can be used in teaching [[organic chemistry]] in an unprecedented way.<ref name="Cable"> He has also co-written a book with Harold Wittcoff showing the linkage between industrial practices and the principles of organic chemistry "Organic Chemistry Principles and Industrial Practice" [http://engineering.nyu.edu/cable/issue/summer-2013/news/faculty/top-down-teaching Cable], ''Top Down Teaching''</ref><ref>[http://sciencewriters.ca/2013/02/04/lessons-from-self-publishing-a-science-textbook-by-mark-m-green/ ''Lessons from self-publishing a science textbook by Mark M. Green''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150105113330/http://sciencewriters.ca/2013/02/04/lessons-from-self-publishing-a-science-textbook-by-mark-m-green/ |date=January 5, 2015 }}, Canadian Science Writers' Association</ref>

==Early life==
Green was born on the [[Lower East Side]] of [[Manhattan]] and grew up in a low-income project in [[Brooklyn]] where he attended local schools. He attended [[City College of New York]] from 1954 to 1958.<ref name="Michigan" />

His grandfather, Mordecai Grunglaz (became Green in the United States), was driven out of [[Belarus]] in 1910 for his involvement in violent resistance to a [[pogrom]] that led to the death of a [[Cossack]]. This separated him from his family so that he missed the birth of his son, Irving Green, the father of Mark. The family was reunited in 1920 in [[Mineville, New York]].<ref>{{cite book| last1=Green| first1=Emanuel |year=1967| title=''My Fringed Garment''| language=he| publisher=Machbarot LeSifrut| others=translated into English by D. Luski and K. Cohen in 2006}}</ref>

He has a sister, Dorothy Lederman, and a brother, Stuart Green, who is founder and director of the New Jersey Coalition for Bullying Awareness and Prevention,<ref>[http://www.lawline.com/faculty/bio.php?id=1448 Lawline], Faculty Information, Stuart Green</ref> a networking organization formed in 2000 in response to the bullying-related [[Columbine High School massacre|tragedy at Columbine]].<ref>[http://www.nj.com/independentpress/index.ssf/2011/05/stuart_green_overlook_social_w.html NY.com], ''Stuart Green, Overlook social worker honored by professional organization for anti-bullying advocacy''</ref>

==Career==
After graduation in 1958 he worked as a technician for [[Pfizer]] Corporation in [[Brooklyn]] and then entered the [[United States Army]] for six months of [[active duty]] in [[Fort McClellan]], [[Alabama]], teaching aspects of [[chemical and biological warfare]].

After fulfilling his service requirements, he worked first for [[Perkin-Elmer Corporation]] in [[Norwalk, Connecticut]], as a technical sales trainee and then for [[Olin Corporation|Olin Mathieson Corporation]] in [[Hartford, Connecticut]], as a technician.

After graduate studies at night at the [[University of Saint Joseph (Connecticut)|Saint Joseph College for Women]] in Hartford, he entered [[New York University]] for full-time study. He left NYU in 1964 to accompany Professor [[Kurt Mislow]] to [[Princeton University]], where Green was awarded a [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) fellowship.

From 1965 to 1966, he studied at Princeton. He graduated in 1966 with a PhD in organic chemistry. Kurt Mislow served as the [[Adviser|advisor]] on his dissertation, ''The Absolute Configurations of Sulfoxides and Sulfinates''.<ref name="Blog">[http://blogs.poly.edu/markgreen/about/ NYU-Poly blog], ''Science from Away''</ref><ref>[http://catalog.princeton.edu/cgi-bin/Pwebrecon.cgi?=&=&=&=&PID=aunCY22KQE81cezwihId_-QpRBC&BROWSE=1&HC=1&SID=4 Princeton University Library entry], Mark M. Green</ref>

On completion of his doctoral degree, he was awarded a [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) Fellowship for a postdoctoral year at [[Stanford University]], with [[Carl Djerassi]] as his postdoctoral advisor.<ref name="Mediander">[http://www.mediander.com/books/9780615702711/organic-chemistry-principles-in/#!/ ''Mediander''], Mark M. Green</ref> With Djerassi, Green studied the use of [[mass spectrometers]] in analyzing chemicals. He intended a career in industry, but was convinced to switch to an academic career by Djerassi and his experiences at Stanford.

Green was assistant professor of chemistry at the [[University of Michigan]] from 1967 to 1974.<ref name="Michigan">[http://um2017.org/faculty-history/faculty/mark-m-green University of Michigan Faculty History Project], Mark M. Green</ref>

In 1971, he was visiting professor at [[metawikipedia:es:Instituto Químico de Sarriá|Instituto Químico de Sarriá]], [[Barcelona, Spain]].<ref name="Blog" />

In 1972, he was visiting professor at [[Technion]], [[Haifa, Israel]].<ref name="Blog" />

He was assistant professor from 1974 to 1976 at [[Michigan State University]], [[East Lansing, Michigan]].<ref name="Blog" />

From 1976 to 1979, Green was associate professor at [[Clarkson College of Technology]], [[Potsdam, New York]].

He was visiting professor in 1978 at [[Jadavpur University]], [[Calcutta]], and [[National Chemical Laboratory]], [[Poona]], [[India]], having been appointed Indo-American Scholar under the [[Fulbright Program]].<ref name="Blog" />

During the years 1974 to 1979, Green became known internationally for his work on the chemistry of the [[Phase (matter)|gas phase]] [[ion]]s encountered in [[mass spectrometers]]. He was attracted to use stereochemical methods to explore a system in which precise kinetic measurements could be made under conditions where there was no intermolecular exchange of energy and therefore an impossible to define temperature. His work was continuously supported by the General Medical Sciences Program of the NIH, and to some extent by the Petroleum Research Fund administered by the [[American Chemical Society]].

In 1980 Green moved to the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now the [[New York University Tandon School of Engineering]]) as an associate professor.<ref>[https://www.linkedin.com/pub/mark-m-green/67/644/6b5 LinkedIn], Mark M. Green</ref> Shortly thereafter, he began to explore [[stereochemical]] ideas in [[polymers]]. In what became [[Chirality (chemistry)|chiral studies]] of the cooperative nature of polymers he found unexpected phenomena, which have widely influenced work in this area. In 1984, Green was promoted to professor and made a member of the Herman F. Mark Polymer Research Institute.

He received a Japan-US Fellowship in 1989 from the NSF and spent a sabbatical year as visiting professor at [[Osaka University]], [[Toyonaka]], Japan.

He was elected as chair of the [[Gordon Research Conferences|Polymer Chemistry Gordon Conference]] for the year 2000.<ref name="Blog" /><ref>[https://www.grc.org/programs.aspx?id=8719 Gordon Research Conference] (June 10–15, 2000)</ref>

He served for three years on the editorial board of the [[American Chemical Society]] journal [[Macromolecules (journal)|''Macromolecules'']], and he serves on the editorial board of ''Topics in Stereochemistry''.<ref name="Blog" /><ref>[http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/bookSeries/10.1002/SERIES2297/homepage/SeriesEditors.html Wiley Online Library, ''Topics in Stereochemistry'', Editors-in-Chief]</ref>

For a number of years, Green has written a monthly column, "Science from Away", for ''The Inverness Oran'', a [[Cape Breton Island|Cape Breton, Nova Scotia]] newspaper, and ''The WestView News'', a [[Greenwich Village]] newspaper.<ref>[http://westviewnews.org/2014/12/science-from-away-short-science-stories/ WestView News], ''Science from Away''</ref> The articles also appear in the NYU-Poly blog ''Science from Away.''<ref>[http://blogs.poly.edu/markgreen/2014/11/16/236/ NYU-Poly Blog], ''Science from Away''</ref>

From 2008 to 2014, Green (under the name Mordecai Green) acted as story consultant for the long running [[web series]] ''[[The Louise Log]]'' and co-wrote all of season three.<ref>{{IMDb name|id=nm1932610|name=Mordecai Green}}</ref>

===Research===
Green began investigations of the cooperative properties of polymers in 1983 in what is now the New York University Polytechnic School of Engineering. Those efforts have been continuously supported by the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF).<ref name="Blog" /><ref>[http://engineering.nyu.edu/press-release/2010/03/18/tracking-down-mystery-life%E2%80%99s-handedness NYU Press Room], ''Tracking Down the Mysteries of Life's "Handedness"''</ref>

He was awarded the Japan-United States Fellowship by the [[National Science Foundation]] in 1989 to support a sabbatical leave in Japan.

===Professor===
After leaving the University of Michigan, Green was assistant professor at [[Michigan State University]] from 1974 to 1976,<ref name="Michigan" /> and associate professor at [[Clarkson College of Technology]] (now Clarkson University ) from 1976 to 1979.

He is rated a popular teacher, having instructed several thousand undergraduates in his career and guided the academic output of the doctoral theses of nineteen [[Graduate school|graduate students]]. He teaches Organic Chemistry using the [[flip teaching]] method and a textbook he wrote for the purpose ("Organic Chemistry Principles in Context: A Story Telling Historical Approach”). He has recorded videos of a year's worth of lectures, making them available to students on YouTube<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCY4W1FrsK9GvNemF4KPvSJg YouTube], Mark M Green</ref> and Vimeo,<ref>[http://vimeo.com/user19946200 Vimio], Mark M Green</ref> so they can study together with other students ([[peer learning]]).

'''Journal articles: '''

Green has published well over 100 papers. These have been cited close to 9,000 times in the refereed literature according to Google Scholar.<ref name="Google">[https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ahynY3gAAAAJ&hl=en Google Scholar Citations], Mark M. ===Awards and honors===
*In 1978, Green was appointed an Indo-American fellow under the [[Fulbright Program]] supporting a six-month stay in India.
*In 1989, he was awarded a Japan-United States Fellowship by the National Science Foundation to support sabbatical leave in Japan.
*He was granted an [[American Cyanamid]] Faculty Research Award in 1991.
*In 1995, he won a Special Creativity Award from the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF).<ref name="Blog" /><ref name="Mediander" />
*He received a [[Sigma Xi]] Distinguished Research Award in 1995.
*Green was appointed to the editorial board of the [[American Chemical Society]] journal [[Macromolecules (journal)|Macromolecules]] for a three-year term commencing in 1999, and he serves on the editorial board of the series ''Topics in Stereochemistry''.<ref name="Blog" /><ref>[http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/bookSeries/10.1002/SERIES2297/homepage/SeriesEditors.html  Wiley Online Library], ''Topics in Stereochemistry'', Editors-in-Chief</ref>
*He was elected chair<ref name="Mediander" /> of the Gordon Conference on Polymer Chemistry for the year 2000.
*In 2000, he was elected as a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref name="Mediander" /> for "pioneering work in important new areas of polymer science."
*He was Senior fellow of the [[Donald Othmer|Othmer Institute of Interdisciplinary Studies]] at the Polytechnic Institute of New York University, from 2002 to 2005.
*Green was elected as a fellow of the Japanese [[Society of Polymer Science]]<ref name="Mediander" /> for a visit to Japan in 2003, and was elected the winner of the Society of Polymer Science of Japan's award for "outstanding achievement in polymer science and technology" for 2005.<ref name="Mediander" />
*He was awarded a [[Allan Jacobs|Jacobs']] "Excellence in Teaching Award" by the New York University Polytechnic School of Engineering<ref name="Mediander" /> in 2006 for his backwards approach to learning organic chemistry and his textbook with Harold Wittcoff entitled, "Organic Chemistry Principles and Industrial Practice."<ref name="Cable" />

==Personal life==
While assistant professor at the [[University of Michigan]], Green became involved in the [[antiwar movement]] ([[Vietnam]]). This led to him showing his students the NARMIC slides<ref>[http://www.afsc.org/video/automated-air-war ''Automated Air War'' (1972)], The NARMIC slides</ref> prepared by the Society of Friends ([[Quakers]])<ref>[http://www.afsc.org/resource/national-actionresearch-military-industrial-complex-narmic National Action/Research on the Military Industrial Complex (NARMIC)], American Friends Service Committee</ref> at [[Swarthmore College]], showing how the US was using illegal weapons in the war, weapons manufactured by major chemical companies in the US.<ref>[http://westviewnews.org/2014/03/science-from-away-backwards-learning/ WestView News, ''Science from Away: Backwards Learning'']</ref> Based on his antiwar activities, the chemistry department decided that he had lost interest in research, and he was denied tenure. Many of his students expressed their support<ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2706&dat=19721017&id=2QpbAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Ik4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=5137,2347410 ''The Michigan Daily''], Letters to the Editor, October 17, 1972</ref> for him at the time.<ref>{{cite news | title = Michigan U. Professor is Reinstated After Ouster for Showing Antiwar Slides Stirs Campus | newspaper = New York Times | pages = 31 | date = October 15, 1972 }}</ref>

Green has been married three times; to Vivian Green (Greenberg) (m. 1958–1969), two children, Lisa Elaine Green (born 1966) and Emily Beth Green (born 1968); to Janet Mark, M.D., (m. 1974–1979); and to [[Anne Flournoy]] (m. 1985–), two children, Frank Thurston Green (born 1989) and Carla Flournoy Green (born 1992).
